scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.name: Share of refund attempts failing with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db
M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.numerator: Count of refunds with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT
M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.denominator: Count of all refund attempts in payment-db

M-TICKET-RESPONSE-TIME.name: Median time from ticket open to first agent response
M-TICKET-RESPONSE-TIME.end_event: Agent first response recorded in ticket-db

M-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE-RATE.name: Share of support tickets that correspond to a failed/incomplete refund
M-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE-RATE.numerator: Tickets linked to a refund with non-success status in payment-db

F-01.statement: 5 of 5 sampled refund records in payment-db have status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

F-02.statement: ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-NO-SELFSERVICE-CHANNEL.statement: Customers wait because there is no automated channel to get refund-status answers; deploying a chatbot would eliminate the wait.

H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY.statement: The underlying refund payment processing in payment-db is slow, so tickets accumulate because the refund itself has not actually completed, not because of missing communication.

H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY.statement: Ticket response delays stem from support team staffing/triage throughput limits (ticket-db response times), independent of refund status itself.

H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP.statement: Refunds are proceeding on normal timelines but customers lack proactive visibility into progress, so they open tickets purely to ask status, not because of a true process delay.

H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW.statement: The refund process (P-REF) itself has structural inefficiencies (e.g. excess steps/handoffs) that drive both slow payment completion and high ticket volume.

H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE.statement: Refunds fail outright at the payment system because of malformed/invalid IBAN data, so they never complete, which is the real driver of refund-status tickets.

interpretation_history.interpretation: payment-db shows all 5 sampled refund records are in status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, i.e. the refunds themselves never completed because of a data-validation failure, not because they are merely slow or because customers lack status visibility.

ticket-db shows support agents respond to tickets quickly (median 2.0h, well inside the 24h SLA) across 900 tickets, indicating the support team's own triage/response throughput is not the bottleneck behind the ticket backlog.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP's interview statement restates the initial request's framing (wait time -> chatbot) without adding new authoritative evidence; it is the same unverified claim already captured as CL-01, not a new fact about refund processing.

U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS.question: Is the 5-record sample of payment-db refund failures (E-01) representative of the full refund population, given payment-db completeness is UNKNOWN?
U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS.decision_impact: Determines whether IBAN-format failure should be treated as the primary driver of the whole ticket backlog or only a partial contributing factor, which changes solution scope and sizing.
U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS.resolution_path: Query payment-db for the full refund failure distribution and its completeness metadata rather than relying on the 5-record sample.
U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS.safe_placeholder: Treat the 100% failure rate as a preliminary signal from a small sample; do not claim it generalizes to the full refund population until confirmed.

U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.question: What proportion of the 900 tickets in ticket-db (E-02) are specifically about refund status/failures versus other support topics?
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.decision_impact: Without this, the magnitude of ticket-backlog reduction achievable by fixing IBAN failures cannot be sized or prioritized against other backlog causes.
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.resolution_path: Cross-reference ticket records in ticket-db with refund IDs/status in payment-db to measure the overlap.
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.safe_placeholder: Do not size expected backlog reduction from an IBAN fix until the ticket-to-failed-refund correlation is measured.

U-IBAN-FAILURE-ROOT-CAUSE.question: Is the IBAN format failure caused by a structural flaw in the refund process (H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW, e.g. missing input validation) or by isolated external data-entry errors, and is it systemic or one-off?
U-IBAN-FAILURE-ROOT-CAUSE.decision_impact: Determines whether the remediation is a process/validation change in P-REF versus a one-off data cleanup, which changes required tools and scope.
U-IBAN-FAILURE-ROOT-CAUSE.resolution_path: Review the refund process steps and any input-validation logic around IBAN capture in P-REF.
U-IBAN-FAILURE-ROOT-CAUSE.safe_placeholder: Do not propose a specific fix mechanism (validation rule vs. manual data cleanup) until the process step producing malformed IBANs is identified.

A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVENESS.statement: The 5-record sample of refund failures in payment-db (E-01) is representative of the broader population of refunds driving the ticket backlog, not an unrepresentative slice.

A-TICKET-REFUND-TOPIC-ASSUMPTI.statement: The 900 tickets measured for response time (E-02) are predominantly about refund status/failures rather than unrelated support topics.

SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.statement: The link between FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds and refund-status tickets is confirmed on the full dataset before any process fix is committed.
SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.threshold: measured on full DA-PAY/DA-TCK data, not just the 5-record sample
SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.validation_method: Cross-reference payment-db refund status codes with ticket-db ticket records and compute the overlap.

SC-REDUCE-IBAN-FAILURES.statement: Reduce the rate of refunds failing due to IBAN format errors.
SC-REDUCE-IBAN-FAILURES.validation_method: Re-run the payment-db refund_failures query after remediation and recompute the rate.

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers get instant answers about refund status instead of waiting on support tickets (initial request from SH-SUP, CL-01).
symptoms: Customers report waiting a long time for answers about refund status, prompting a request for a chatbot (CL-01, CL-02).
100% of sampled refund records in payment-db (5 of 5) are stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status, i.e. the refund never completes (E-01, F-01).
Refund tickets persist/accumulate even though support agents respond within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets, E-02, F-02).
problem_definition.root_problem: Refund-status tickets accumulate not because support is slow to respond or customers lack a self-service answer channel, but because refunds fail outright at the payment system due to malformed/invalid IBAN data (status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db), so the refund itself never completes and customers keep contacting support about an unresolved refund (E-01, E-02).

trace.summary: Refund-status tickets accumulate not because support is slow to respond or customers lack a self-service answer channel, but because refunds fail outright at the payment system due to malformed/invalid IBAN data (status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db), so the refund itself never completes and customers keep contacting support about an unresolved refund (E-01, E-02).

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Customer submits a refund request that includes IBAN bank details. → Payment system rejects the refund during validation because the IBAN data is malformed/invalid, recording status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01). → Because the refund never completes, the customer receives no confirmation or payment. → Customer opens or follows up on a support ticket asking about refund status. → Support agents respond quickly (median 2.0h, within 24h SLA, E-02), so the ticket is answered but cannot be closed because the underlying refund is still failed. → Unresolved refund-status tickets accumulate, which stakeholders perceive and describe as customers 'waiting' (CL-01, CL-02).; rejected framings: [('H-NO-SELFSERVICE-CHANNEL', 'Contradicted by E-01: refunds are failing outright at the payment system, not merely lacking an automated status-answer channel, so a chatbot would not fix the underlying failure.'), ('H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP', 'Contradicted by E-01: refunds are not proceeding on normal timelines awaiting a visibility fix, they are in a hard FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT state.'), ('H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY', 'Contradicted by E-01: the records show outright failure (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not mere slowness of an otherwise-succeeding process.'), ('H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY', 'Contradicted by E-02: support responds with a 2.0h median, well inside the 24h SLA, so staffing/triage throughput is not the bottleneck.')]
[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS deferred to VOB-U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS; [CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE deferred to VOB-U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE

framing_assertion.rationale: SH-SUP's initial request asserts that building a chatbot will stop customers waiting for refund answers, implying the root cause is a missing self-service answering channel rather than actual refund processing delay.

hypotheses.statement: Customers wait because there is no automated channel to get refund-status answers; deploying a chatbot would eliminate the wait.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's stated framing and justification for the chatbot request; SH-SUP's noted bias is to frame everything as response speed, so this framing itself needs testing rather than adoption.

hypotheses.statement: The underlying refund payment processing in payment-db is slow, so tickets accumulate because the refund itself has not actually completed, not because of missing communication.
hypotheses.rationale: If refund execution is the bottleneck, a chatbot answering 'where is my refund' would not shorten actual wait time; the fix would need to target P-REF processing speed.
discriminating_evidence: correlation between ticket open time and payment-db refund stage

hypotheses.statement: Ticket response delays stem from support team staffing/triage throughput limits (ticket-db response times), independent of refund status itself.
hypotheses.rationale: If the bottleneck is agent capacity rather than information availability, a chatbot could help only if it actually deflects ticket volume, which is a different success criterion than 'answering questions'.

hypotheses.statement: Refunds are proceeding on normal timelines but customers lack proactive visibility into progress, so they open tickets purely to ask status, not because of a true process delay.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, the fix could be a lighter-weight status notification rather than a full conversational chatbot, changing scope significantly.
discriminating_evidence: timing of ticket creation relative to payment-db refund stage

hypotheses.statement: The refund process (P-REF) itself has structural inefficiencies (e.g. excess steps/handoffs) that drive both slow payment completion and high ticket volume.
hypotheses.rationale: A structural process flaw would require redesigning P-REF steps/handoffs rather than adding a customer-facing tool, which is currently unspecified (P-REF has no recorded steps or handoffs).

actions.question: What do ticket-db response-time records show about current support response/backlog patterns and whether ticket volume is dominated by pure status-check requests?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether delays trace to support triage throughput (response times) versus tickets being pure status-asks, directly testing the two hypotheses that name ticket-db response times as the mechanism.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY is rated HIGH decision_impact and this is the authoritative data asset (DA-TCK) it names; result changes whether staffing/triage is the fix target.
actions.why_now: No ticket-level data has been pulled yet (already_executed is empty) and this is the catalog item that most directly names the mechanism H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY claims.

actions.question: What do payment-db refund-failure records show about the frequency and causes of delayed or failed refund processing?
actions.expected_information_gain: Shows whether refunds are actually stalled/failing in payment-db, which is the exact mechanism H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY (CRITICAL) claims, and whether failure patterns suggest structural process steps/handoffs (H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW).
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY carries CRITICAL decision_impact; confirming or rejecting it determines whether a chatbot (communication fix) is even relevant versus a payment-pipeline fix.
actions.why_now: This is the authoritative data asset (DA-PAY) that literally names 'refund payment processing in payment-db' as the mechanism H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY describes; no payment data has been checked yet.

actions.question: What does bank-api settlement status show about whether refund delays originate at the external settlement stage versus within the internal refund process?
actions.expected_information_gain: Separates whether slow settlement is caused by the external bank step (supporting H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY as a settlement issue) or by internal process handoffs (supporting H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW), since neither hypothesis specifies which stage.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW is CRITICAL; without settlement data it cannot be distinguished from H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY, both of which point to the same P-REF process.
actions.why_now: This external tool is the only catalog item covering the settlement leg of P-REF and has not been queried; it is needed to separate the two CRITICAL hypotheses that both implicate payment delay.

actions.question: Ask SH-SUP to describe the actual refund process steps/handoffs in P-REF and whether any self-service refund-status channel currently exists.
actions.expected_information_gain: Provides qualitative detail on P-REF structure (steps/handoffs) and existence of a self-service channel, which no tool-query data asset covers, informing H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW and H-NO-SELFSERVICE-CHANNEL.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: No catalog data asset describes process steps or channel existence; this is the only available source, though SH-SUP's noted bias toward framing issues as 'response speed' limits reliability.
actions.why_now: SH-SUP is the only source for process-step and channel-existence facts not captured by any tool-query data asset, and this is a stakeholder claim (CL-01) still unverified.

proposal.stop_reason: All four catalog items are proposed and each has been matched to the live hypothesis whose named mechanism it most directly addresses: ticket-db response_times to H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY, payment-db refund_failures to H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY, bank-api settlement_status to the payment-delay/process-flaw split, and the SH-SUP interview to H-NO-SELFSERVICE-CHANNEL/H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW; no catalog item remains unchecked against any still-live hypothesis.

hypothesis_effects.rationale: The hypothesis frames the problem as the refund being slow/not yet completed, but the records show outright FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status, a hard validation failure rather than a pending/slow process.

The observation concerns payment-db refund outcomes, not ticket-db response/triage throughput.

proposal.root_problem: Refund-status tickets accumulate not because support is slow to respond or customers lack a self-service answer channel, but because refunds fail outright at the payment system due to malformed/invalid IBAN data (status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db), so the refund itself never completes and customers keep contacting support about an unresolved refund (E-01, E-02).
proposal.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers get instant answers about refund status instead of waiting on support tickets (initial request from SH-SUP, CL-01).
symptoms: Customers report waiting a long time for answers about refund status, prompting a request for a chatbot (CL-01, CL-02).
100% of sampled refund records in payment-db (5 of 5) are stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status, i.e. the refund never completes (E-01, F-01).
Refund tickets persist/accumulate even though support agents respond within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets, E-02, F-02).
causal_chain: Customer submits a refund request that includes IBAN bank details.
Payment system rejects the refund during validation because the IBAN data is malformed/invalid, recording status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
Because the refund never completes, the customer receives no confirmation or payment.
Customer opens or follows up on a support ticket asking about refund status.
Support agents respond quickly (median 2.0h, within 24h SLA, E-02), so the ticket is answered but cannot be closed because the underlying refund is still failed.
Unresolved refund-status tickets accumulate, which stakeholders perceive and describe as customers 'waiting' (CL-01, CL-02).

assumptions.statement: The 5-record sample of refund failures in payment-db (E-01) is representative of the broader population of refunds driving the ticket backlog, not an unrepresentative slice.
The 900 tickets measured for response time (E-02) are predominantly about refund status/failures rather than unrelated support topics.

key_points: The initial request from SH-SUP (support lead) was "build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds" (CL-01, CL-02); this is a stakeholder claim/framing, not a confirmed fact.

Investigation found that 5 of 5 sampled payment-db refund records are stuck in status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, meaning the refunds never complete due to a data-validation failure, not a communication gap (E-01, F-01).
ticket-db shows support agents respond to tickets quickly (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets), so slow support response is not the bottleneck (E-02, F-02).

Based on this, the root problem was redefined (PD-1): refund tickets accumulate because refunds fail outright at the payment system from malformed IBAN data, not because support is slow or customers lack a self-service channel.

Hypothesis H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE is SUPPORTED by E-01/E-02; the chatbot-fixes-it hypothesis (H-NO-SELFSERVICE-CHANNEL), a slow-processing hypothesis (H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY), a status-visibility hypothesis (H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP), and a support-triage-capacity hypothesis (H-SUPPORT-TRIAGE-CAPACITY) were all REJECTED based on E-01/E-02/E-03.

The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two critical unknowns (U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS, U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE) as open verification obligations (VOB-U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS, VOB-U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE), both outside the released scope.

The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no items on hold; the released scope was limited to investigating the IBAN validation process in P-REF, as reflected in solution_design's release_scope and minimum_useful_scope.

A structural fix to add IBAN validation at refund intake (SR-IBAN-INPUT-VALIDATION-FIX) was identified as the way to remove the root cause but could not be executed in this run because no domain_authorizations exist to modify P-REF.
limitations_explained: The conclusion that IBAN-format failures drive the ticket backlog rests on a small sample of only 5 payment-db records, and the completeness of payment-db relative to the full refund population is UNKNOWN (VOB-U-SAMPLE-COMPLETENESS, open, outside release scope).

It is not yet confirmed what proportion of the 900 ticket-db tickets are actually about refund status/failures versus other topics, so the strength of the ticket-to-refund link is unverified (VOB-U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE, open, outside release scope).

Whether the IBAN format failures are a systemic process design flaw (H-PROCESS-DESIGN-FLAW) or isolated/one-off data-entry errors remains an open question (U-IBAN-FAILURE-ROOT-CAUSE, VOB-R-3), though this is flagged as non-critical for this release.
The bank-api tool needed to check settlement_status is DEGRADED (ACCESS_DENIED, not transient, no fallback), so IBAN-failure diagnosis via that channel is incomplete.

No domain authorizations exist to modify the refund intake process (P-REF), so the proposed structural fix (adding/strengthening IBAN validation, SR-IBAN-INPUT-VALIDATION-FIX) could not be executed in this run.
The DEFINE gate result itself was only a CONDITIONAL_PASS, with the two sample-completeness and ticket-linkage unknowns formally deferred as VOBs rather than resolved.
proposal.summary: The support lead's original request was for a chatbot to stop customers waiting on refund status (CL-01/CL-02), but investigation of payment-db and ticket-db reframed the problem: all 5 sampled refund records are stuck failing with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), and support's own response time is well within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h, E-02), so the real driver of the ticket backlog is refunds failing outright at the payment system due to bad IBAN data, not slow support or missing self-service. This supported hypothesis H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE and rejected the chatbot-based and other alternative explanations. The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two critical unknowns about sample representativeness and ticket-refund linkage to open verification obligations outside the released scope. The final decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION (nothing held): the release covers investigation of the IBAN validation issue in process P-REF, but does not include the full-population confirmation, the ticket-correlation analysis, or the actual process fix, all of which remain open/unfinished.
